title: Gemini 4 Carbon reaches paid API users and begins its Ultra rollout
summary: Google’s November 10 update opens Carbon to paid API users and starts an Ultra rollout. Carbon for cyber remains a Fairwind route, and public-model introductory pricing expires November 30. Earlier benchmark claims still need task-specific validation.

sections.title: The November 10 update changes who can start
sections.html:
Google’s November 10 availability announcement materially changes the adoption decision for Gemini 4 Carbon. The October 28 launch began with selected cybersecurity defenders. Google now announces API availability for paying developers and enterprises through AI Studio and Gemini for business, alongside a rollout to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Antigravity, the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search. The earlier conclusion that general access was still ahead is therefore superseded. This is documented availability, not an account-level access test by AI Observatory.

Three boundaries remain useful. Paid API access is different from a free API tier; an Ultra rollout is different from every account already displaying the model; and Carbon for cyber still has a separate Fairwind application route. A team can now plan an ordinary coding evaluation around a named access path, while confirming entitlement in its own account. This report does not verify regional coverage, quotas, the API model identifier or every product’s rollout completion.

The practical change is that a prepared experiment can move toward execution. It does not establish that Carbon will outperform another model on a particular project, nor that a longer autonomous session is worthwhile. Retain a working baseline, define what counts as an accepted result and start with a reversible task. The original launch date remains October 28 in this report’s history; November 10 is the new availability event, and this revision reflects evidence retrieved November 11.

sections.title: Keep historical benchmarks attached to their conditions
sections.html:
At the October 28 launch, Google reported 88.2 percent on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8 percent on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0 percent on CWE-bench for patching. It explicitly described those external benchmark evaluations as conducted without guardrails. These historical results remain evidence of what Google reported under that setup. They are not measurements of the newly accessible public service, and they do not show which security tasks that service permits.

The launch benchmark image was visually inspected during the earlier research. It showed Carbon below GPT-6 Astra on FrontierSWE 2 and below Claude Opus 5.5 on the OSWorld-2.1 offline subset. That unevenness remains a useful warning against choosing a model from a headline ranking. The table is a publisher comparison rather than an independent Observatory reproduction. Its methodology destination could not be inspected after a navigation timeout and the failed recovery attempt.

The availability change should not silently refresh these results into a November performance test. No Carbon task was executed for either edition. For a meaningful comparison, use the same repository snapshot, task instructions, tool permissions and acceptance criteria for each candidate. Keep unsuccessful runs in the record, and distinguish a plausible explanation from a patch that survives review. Benchmark evidence can identify a question worth asking; observed outcomes on representative work must answer the operational question.

sections.title: Measure sustained work by accepted progress
sections.html:
Google’s original launch described internal engineering investigations that persisted for days through dead ends, including root-cause analysis and patching across large repositories. That statement concerns internal use, not a guaranteed unattended runtime. Longer persistence can discover a useful path, but it can also repeat an incorrect premise. A team evaluating Carbon should measure progress and correctness alongside elapsed time, rather than treating session duration as an achievement.

The November article also previews Antigravity’s /swarm coordination and describes Carbon taking demanding reasoning roles alongside lighter models. This is an orchestration preview, not proof that every paid API caller receives an equivalent agent system. A model endpoint alone does not provide repository isolation, task scheduling, browser inspection or a reliable handoff between workers. Before a multi-agent experiment, establish who owns each file, how conflicting patches are resolved and which component decides that the work is complete.

For a first trial, select a historical engineering issue whose accepted fix and regression tests are known. Supply the pre-fix repository and symptom report while keeping the accepted solution out of the working context. Require a diagnosis, a bounded patch and actual test results. Record token charges, tool time, abandoned approaches and human review. Stop when the spending ceiling is reached or evidence shows the original assumption is wrong. This proposed evaluation has not been run here; it is a way to turn the new access into an inspectable adoption decision.

sections.title: New documentation does not turn finite tests into immunity
sections.html:
The October launch reported zero successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 while attempts remained at 0.4 percent, and zero attack success on the evaluated Gray Swan indirect prompt-injection benchmark. The two distinctions still matter: an unsuccessful attempt is not the absence of an attempt, and a finite evaluation is not a universal failure rate. Wider availability does not change the scope of those historical measurements.

The November announcement now links a Carbon-specific Safety and Security report and a model card. That is a meaningful documentation change from the earlier reliance on Argon background material. Neither linked document was inspected for this revision, so their presence is recorded without claiming their contents have been verified. The article itself acknowledges that sophisticated prompt-injection attacks still expose room for improvement. Its discussion of mitigations should be read as Google’s account, not as an Observatory security certification.

A practical acceptance test should include an incomplete task. Supply a missing dependency or an intentionally unavailable fixture and check whether the model reports the limitation, distinguishes attempted tests from passed tests and avoids inventing outputs. Introduce harmless conflicting instructions in a controlled repository to examine scope handling. Preserve the actual commands and results for review. An honest partial answer can be more valuable than a polished but unsupported completion claim. No adversarial test, cyber tool execution or independent safety evaluation was performed during this research.

sections.title: Public Carbon and Carbon for cyber have different routes
sections.html:
The November update continues to direct cybersecurity defenders to the Fairwind Program for Carbon for cyber on a rolling basis. The public API announcement therefore should not be treated as automatic entitlement to the specialist cyber offering. Ask which model and deployment surface an agreement covers, what work is permitted and which data-handling terms apply before planning a security workflow around it.

The Fairwind page saved on October 28 described organizational due diligence, access tracking and restrictions on sharing or reselling access. Its technology and retention answers still referred to Argon at that inspection. Those are historical observations, not a claim about the page’s current wording: it was not revisited for this revision. An Argon-specific zero-retention answer remains insufficient evidence for Carbon terms, and the new public rollout does not repair that contractual gap.

There is also a research-access route. Google says the existing scientist program is expanding to include Carbon, with six months of access through Antigravity’s highest usage tier for selected participants. Applications and rolling onboarding remain conditional on eligibility, capacity and selection. This is a chance to apply, not a universal student or teacher entitlement. An eligible lab can prepare a bounded proposal using non-sensitive materials and an answer key. A classroom needing predictable access should confirm its actual account arrangement before making the model a required part of an assignment.

sections.title: Budget for the dated public-model price change
sections.html:
The November announcement gives public Carbon introductory API rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Its footnote now supplies the previously missing deadline: the introductory period expires November 30, 2026, after which $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens apply. The footnote explicitly limits this statement to the Carbon model intended for public access. It is not evidence of Fairwind pricing or a change to the Ultra subscription fee.

For an illustrative workload of one million uncached input tokens and one hundred thousand output tokens, the stated token rates imply $3 during the introductory period and $6 afterward. This is arithmetic, not an invoice or a price for a completed engineering task. It excludes tool execution, storage, infrastructure, retries and other contract conditions. The earlier launch mentioned a cached-input discount; this revision does not assume that detail settles the current cache billing rules on every service surface.

Use the later rate when considering a workflow that will continue beyond the promotion. Count all attempts needed to reach an accepted result, including reviewer time. A long investigation can justify its cost when it resolves a difficult fault, but a low headline token rate does not establish that outcome. Check the applicable billing page and account limits before committing a workload. This research inspected the public article and its footnote, without authenticating into billing, testing quotas or verifying a complete commercial schedule.

sections.title: Turn access into small education, app and website trials
sections.html:
For education, start with a teacher-curated set of public source documents and a known answer key. Ask Carbon to produce a short explanation with source references, then have learners verify each factual step and identify unsupported claims. Keep the teacher’s corrections as an inspectable output. The failure to watch for is fluent synthesis that hides a missing premise. A non-user version of the lesson can compare the October and November announcements to distinguish a launch, an access expansion and a price expiry.

For an app team, provide a disposable repository copy, a reproducible bug and a narrow acceptance set. One example is a form that loses entered data after a failed request. Require the model to explain the cause, patch the behavior and demonstrate that validation and retry behavior still work. Integrating the API into a coding loop requires explicit tool permissions, output handling, time limits and a path for stopping with partial findings. No ready-made integration or successful app repair is claimed here.

For a website team, turn an approved content outline into an interactive explanation whose claims link back to source material. Review the rendered page at narrow and wide widths, tab through its controls and test missing-data states. Google’s new article describes web-development demonstrations using build-and-check loops, but those vendor examples do not establish accessibility or correctness for a new site. Keep visual acceptance separate from data and behavior checks. A convincing screen can still conceal a broken submission or an inaccessible control. The useful output is a reviewable change with verified behavior, not merely an attractive preview.

sections.title: Video work still needs a defined production boundary
sections.html:
A video producer can evaluate Carbon on the software around production: a caption-processing script, a media manifest or a failing render pipeline. Supply a small fixture with known source files, expected timecodes and frame-rate assumptions. Ask for a bounded repair and a comparison against expected outputs, including a missing-asset case. Inspect caption synchronization in the production tool and retain the originals. The likely failure is a plausible code change that shifts timing or mishandles an input format.

The November article adds creative demonstrations involving Antigravity, Blender and Three.js, including a scene built from a video reference supplied by another model. This supports investigating Carbon as a coding and coordination component. It does not establish native Carbon video generation, speech synthesis, editable timeline export or ownership terms for every asset in such a pipeline. Linked demonstrations were not run or independently audited for this report. Creative quality and rights clearance still require their own review.

The updated adoption decision is consequently more actionable: readers with the announced paid API or eligible subscription route can check entitlement and try a bounded task, while cyber defenders follow Fairwind. Start with an existing baseline and a stopping rule, then compare accepted outputs and observed costs. The public rollout removes the earlier blanket access obstacle. It leaves the central performance question open: whether Carbon solves the reader’s actual problem reliably enough to justify the integration, supervision and ongoing price.

useCases: Teacher-reviewed source synthesis and evidence-literacy exercises
Website behavior, accessibility and source-link reviews
limitations: Paid API and Ultra availability are publisher announcements; account entitlement, regions, quotas and model identifiers were not tested.
Carbon for cyber remains a separate Fairwind application route; public-model prices do not establish specialist terms.
No Carbon execution, independent benchmark reproduction or authenticated billing check.
Historical benchmark methodology was not inspected; November model card, safety report and linked demonstrations were not opened.
Fairwind observations date to October 28 and remained Argon-specific then; no current Carbon retention promise is inferred.
November evidence comes from a saved web.open full-page fallback after Chrome transport was unavailable, not a successful Chrome revisit.

sources.supports: November 10 paid API availability, Ultra rollout, separate cyber and scientist routes, public-model price expiry, and clearly attributed documentation/demo observations

judgment: A material access expansion makes bounded paid-API and eligible-subscription trials actionable. Carbon for cyber remains separately controlled; task performance, integration effort and full commercial terms still need direct evaluation.
researchNote: This revision uses the saved full-page November 10 Google announcement retrieved November 11 through web.open after Chrome transport was unavailable. Historical launch, Fairwind and benchmark-image observations remain dated October 28. No live model, linked demo, model card, safety report, cyber tool or billing account was tested for the update.
